subtitle: Acceptance involves understanding cultural differences in context while still making reasoned judgments. Use that understanding to examine DHS decisions with the people affected and the staff responsible for review.
audience: For DHS and DSD supervisors, policy and program staff, case managers, HR partners and communications staff who make or shape decisions affecting diverse communities. The Minimization course in this series is helpful background but not required.

lessons.title: Naming Acceptance: seeing patterns of difference and commonality
objectives: Describe Acceptance as the first intercultural mindset on the Intercultural Development Continuum.
Distinguish recognizing a cultural difference from agreeing with it or judging it.
Explain the gap the continuum names between recognizing difference and being able to adapt to it.
Identify the ethical challenge that can arise when several cultural approaches all make sense.
lessons.teaching:
This is the fourth course in the program's six-part series on the Intercultural Development Continuum. The continuum, published by IDI, LLC, moves from the monocultural mindsets of Denial and Polarization, through the transitional orientation of Minimization, to the intercultural mindsets of Acceptance and Adaptation. The program's series closes with Integration, drawn from Milton Bennett's earlier Developmental Model of Intercultural Sensitivity. Acceptance is where attention shifts from what people share to how culture shapes what they do, while commonality stays in view.

The continuum describes Acceptance as an orientation in which people recognize and appreciate patterns of cultural difference and commonality in their own and other cultures. The description includes one’s own culture: in Acceptance, people start to see their own habits of communication, decision-making and respect as cultural patterns, not as the neutral baseline. It also describes curiosity, with an interest in learning how a pattern of behavior makes sense within a different cultural community, rather than treating it as a strange exception to a normal rule. Bennett describes this as experiencing others as equally complex but different in form.

Acceptance does not mean agreeing with everything. Bennett is explicit that accepting the reality of a cultural difference is not the same as approving of it; a difference can still be judged negatively. What changes is how the judgment is made. Instead of measuring others against one's own cultural standard without noticing, a person in Acceptance tries first to understand the practice in its own context. In public service, understanding context helps staff identify relevant questions without guessing what a person needs or what a rule permits. Applicable legal duties and individual circumstances still require review by the responsible staff.

The continuum also names two limits. People in Acceptance are curious and appreciative but may not yet be fully able to adapt their own behavior to cultural difference. Hearing that someone wants family involved does not establish how a meeting should run or what information may be shared. Ask the person about their preferences and confirm relevant decision-making and disclosure authority. And because people in Acceptance can see the value in many approaches, choosing one can be hard, which can show up as hesitation when a decision must be made across cultural groups. As in the whole series, this course uses the continuum as shared vocabulary. It does not administer the Intercultural Development Inventory or infer anyone’s result from behavior. A qualified administrator administers the inventory and shares individual results in a confidential one-to-one debrief; that role does not authorize guessing. The cases here are fictional, and no colleague or community member is expected to represent an entire group.
lessons.keyPoint: Acceptance means recognizing and being curious about cultural patterns, including your own, without assuming they must match yours. Recognition is not the same as agreement, and it is not yet the ability to adapt.
lessons.example: Practice case: In a county partnership meeting, Megan, a DSD policy analyst, hears a Tribal social services director, Darrell, explain that some families in his community prefer that initial conversations about services happen through a respected relative before any formal meeting with the state. Megan is genuinely curious and asks thoughtful questions about why. Afterward, her team drafts an outreach plan. Megan realizes the plan still begins with a letter from the state inviting the person to a scheduled meeting. She understood the practice, but she is not sure what to change or whether she is allowed to change it.
lessons.question: What is the most useful next step for Megan?
choices: Rewrite the outreach plan herself around what she heard, since she now understands the community's practice.
Leave the plan as is, since her curiosity was respectful and the letter meets the requirement.

Bring the gap to her team and ask how to engage Darrell and the Tribal partner on options, routing any government-to-government questions through the department's Tribal relations and consultation process.
feedback: Understanding one conversation is not enough to redesign a plan for a sovereign nation's members. Acting alone risks replacing one assumption with another.
Curiosity without follow-through is the gap this lesson names. The requirement may be met, but the plan still may not reach the people it is meant for.
This is the strongest response. Megan names the gap between recognizing and adapting, involves her team and the partner, and respects formal Tribal consultation channels.
lessons.reflection: Think of a time you felt genuinely curious about a difference at work. What did you do with that curiosity afterward, and what, if anything, changed in your practice?
lessons.action: Using Megan’s fictional case, identify one assumption in the outreach process and one question for the responsible team. Explain how they could seek input without assuming that one conversation represents a whole nation or community.

check.question: In Bennett's description of Acceptance, what is the relationship between accepting a cultural difference and agreeing with it?
check.correct: They are different: a person can recognize and understand a difference in context and still judge it negatively.
wrong: They are the same: accepting a difference means approving of it.
Acceptance means no longer making any judgments at all.
check.feedback: Acceptance changes how judgments are made, not whether they are made. The person first seeks to understand the practice in its own context instead of measuring it against an unnoticed personal standard. Judgment remains necessary, especially where laws and safety standards apply.

lessons.title: Connecting curiosity with team decisions
objectives: Identify signs that a team recognizes cultural difference but has not yet built it into its default practice.
Compare learning activities that increase curiosity with practice changes that affect decisions.
Explain why a team's knowledge about communities can remain separate from its decisions.
Draft a way to link what a team has learned to a specific process or decision point.
lessons.teaching:
A team may show curiosity about cultural differences while its working practices remain unchanged. That observation invites questions; it does not establish an inventory result. People are interested in the communities they serve. They attend cultural learning events, invite speakers, read community material and talk respectfully about difference. They can explain why a practice makes sense in context. What is often missing is the connection between that knowledge and the team's defaults. The intake script, the service planning template, the hiring panel questions and the timeline for public comment may look exactly as they did before the learning began.

Possible explanations include the authority, time and coordination needed to change a process. Participation in this course is voluntary, while assigned agency training may be required. Staff may worry that adapting to one group means treating people unequally, or that there is no clear rule permitting the change. Others may see many valid approaches and hesitate to pick one, which the continuum names as a real challenge of Acceptance. Check the actual reasons for an unchanged process and its effects; neither intent nor outcomes can be inferred from attendance at learning events.

Some signs to watch for in DHS and DSD work: cultural learning shows up in presentations but not in the equity analysis for a decision. Community partners are thanked for their insight but rarely see how it changed anything. Staff know that certain families prefer in-person conversation, but the only outreach channel is a mailed notice. Interpreters are available, but meetings are still scheduled at times and in formats set without asking the family. A team may also describe itself as "culturally aware" as though awareness were the outcome, rather than the starting point for better service.

To move from noticing to linking, pick a specific decision point and ask: what do we now know about the people affected that we did not know before, and where in this process does it change what we do? The cited 2023 DHS Equity Policy sets responsibilities for engagement and equity analysis. It describes an approved analysis or scan for specified long-term-impact actions submitted for approval, including a customized tool developed with an equity director. The statewide quick guide offers related questions, but it is distinct from the agency’s approved process. Confirm the current requirements with responsible staff. The aim is not to adapt everything at once. It is to make sure that learning shows up somewhere concrete, and that partners can see the difference their input made.
lessons.keyPoint: A team can be curious and knowledgeable about difference while its forms, meetings and timelines stay the same. Link learning to a specific decision point so it changes practice.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD unit held a well-attended series of lunch sessions with speakers from East African, Latino and Hmong community organizations. Staff describe the sessions as eye-opening. Six months later, Jae, a program specialist, is updating the unit's public input process for a proposed service rate change. The process still offers a single online comment form in English, open for thirty days, with a webinar during the workday. Jae remembers a speaker explaining that many people in her community learn about changes through community radio and trusted organizations.
lessons.question: What should Jae do?
choices: Propose that the unit revisit the input process with the Equity Analysis Toolkit, adding options suggested by partners, such as working with trusted organizations and offering translated and spoken ways to comment, within the rules that govern the comment period.
Send the lunch speakers a link to the online form and ask them to share it.
Assume the comment period rules make any change impossible and keep the existing process.
feedback: This is the strongest response. Jae links what the unit learned to a specific process, uses the department's method, and respects the formal rules for public comment while expanding how people can participate.

Sharing a link may help some people, but it does not address the language and participation barriers described in the case. Ask partners what support they can offer without making them responsible for the agency’s access duties.

Check the actual public-comment requirements with the responsible staff before deciding what can change. Preserve required notices and deadlines while considering additional lawful ways to participate.
lessons.reflection: What is one thing your team has learned about the people you serve in the past year? Where, if anywhere, can you see it in how the team actually works?
lessons.action: Pick one process your team owns. Write one sentence naming something the team has learned about the people it affects, and one sentence naming where in the process that learning could change a step. Share it with your supervisor or team.

check.question: Which sign best suggests a team is recognizing difference but not yet adapting to it?
check.correct: Staff can explain why communities' practices make sense, but the team's forms, outreach and meeting formats have not changed.
wrong: Staff dismiss cultural differences as unimportant.
Staff say the team's way of doing things is better than other ways.
check.feedback: The keyed response describes the gap tested in this lesson: recognition has not changed practice. It does not establish the team’s orientation or explain why the process stayed the same. Examine authority, resources, access and feedback before choosing a next step.

lessons.title: Reflecting on curiosity, decisions and follow-through
objectives: Identify signs in your own work of curiosity that has not yet translated into changed behavior.
Distinguish thoughtful openness from hesitation that avoids making a needed decision.
Explain how to make a decision across cultural perspectives that is grounded in context rather than one's own cultural standard.
Plan one specific behavior to practice in a real work situation.
lessons.teaching:
Reflection on curiosity is most useful when it concerns specific work. You might understand a partner’s explanation yet remain unsure what authority you have to change a process. You might also recognize a communication habit of your own that others experience differently. Neither observation establishes an orientation. This lesson offers three ways to examine what happens when a decision needs attention.

First, consider whether your questions in partner meetings lead you to examine the plans you later draft. Do you know that a person you serve prefers to include family in decisions, yet schedule the meeting in a way that makes that hard? Rather than treating this as a moral failure, investigate whether knowledge, authority, resources or another constraint is preventing an appropriate response.

Second, consider whether hesitation is preventing a needed decision. The continuum describes a challenge in seeing merit in several approaches while still needing to choose among them. In public service, though, not deciding is also a decision, and it often defaults to the existing process. Bennett describes the developmental task here as finding a basis for judgment that is not ethnocentric: first understanding each perspective in its own context, then making and owning a commitment. For services covered by chapter 245D, section 245D.07 sets person-centered service duties for license holders. The Positive Supports Rule also has a defined scope; these provisions are not blanket instructions for every DHS decision. Identify the relevant program, decision-making authority and applicable requirements with responsible staff. Understanding context does not replace that review.

Third, consider whose perspective receives your attention and whether you overlook colleagues whose communication styles differ from your preferences. Acceptance includes seeing your own group's variety and your own culture as one pattern among many.

As with every course in this series, this reflection is private and practical. It is not a way to place yourself on the continuum or to assign yourself a stage. If you want a formal view of your orientation, the Intercultural Development Inventory is available only through a licensed Qualified Administrator, with a debrief. What you can do this week is pick a specific behavior, practice it, and ask for feedback.
lessons.keyPoint: Honest reflection on Acceptance asks what you do with your curiosity: whether it reaches your decisions, and whether respect for many views has turned into avoiding a needed choice.
lessons.example: Practice case: Rosa, a DSD policy consultant, is drafting guidance on how lead agencies should involve families in support planning. Community members have described very different preferences: some families want the person served to lead with minimal family role, others expect elders to be central, and some disabled self-advocates want firm protection of the person's own voice. Rosa sees merit in all of it. The draft is two weeks late because she keeps revising to avoid favoring any view.
lessons.question: What is the most useful way for Rosa to move forward?
choices: Keep revising until every community member is fully satisfied with the language.

Center the person’s preferences and participation, check applicable planning and decision-making authority, and explain how different family roles can be supported within those requirements. Take the draft to the supervisor and responsible legal or policy staff.
Pick the approach that matches how her own family makes decisions, since she understands it best.
feedback: Seeking full agreement from every perspective can become the hesitation this lesson describes. The guidance is still needed, and delay usually keeps the old default in place.

This is the strongest response. It protects the person’s participation while checking applicable authority, privacy and planning requirements. Family expectations alone do not establish who may decide or receive information.
Choosing by one's own cultural standard is the ethnocentric basis for judgment that Acceptance moves away from, even when it is unintentional.
lessons.reflection: Is there a decision at work you have been putting off because several perspectives all seem reasonable? What would a grounded, explainable choice look like?
lessons.action: Use Rosa’s fictional case to draft a question about participation, decision-making authority or disclosure. Name the responsible role that could resolve it and a realistic next step without collecting actual case information.

check.question: What does Bennett describe as the developmental task for someone in Acceptance facing a decision across cultural perspectives?
check.correct: Understanding each perspective in context and then making and owning an ethical commitment that is not simply based on one's own cultural standard.
wrong: Avoiding decisions until every cultural group agrees.
Treating all practices as equally acceptable so no judgment is needed.
check.feedback: Acceptance can drift into paralysis or into the idea that anything goes. Bennett's framing asks for both: understand context first, then commit. In DHS work, that commitment also sits inside laws, rules and program requirements that the responsible offices interpret.

lessons.title: From recognizing to adapting: applying Acceptance to DHS decisions
objectives: Explain what separates Acceptance from Adaptation on the continuum.
Plan how to turn a recognized cultural difference into a specific change in a DHS or DSD decision.
Compare adapting a process with lowering a standard or making an unofficial exception.
Identify when a formal office, such as EOAD, the ADA coordinator, legal counsel or Tribal consultation, must be involved.
lessons.teaching:
The continuum describes Adaptation as the orientation in which people can shift perspective and adjust behavior in culturally appropriate and authentic ways. Acceptance builds the recognition; Adaptation builds the capacity to act. The bridge between them is practice: using what you understand in real situations, getting feedback and adjusting. The next course in this series explores Adaptation in depth. This lesson focuses on the first steps across that bridge in everyday department decisions.

A useful sequence has four moves. Recognize: identify an observed practice or concern and any assumptions you are making. Do not assign a cultural explanation from someone’s name or group membership. Understand: learn, from the people affected and from partners, how the pattern makes sense and what it means for this decision. Ask what the purpose requires: distinguish a legal requirement from a familiar method or an assumption about the rule. Review both with responsible staff. ADA Title II can require reasonable modifications to policies, practices or procedures, subject to the fundamental-alteration limit; unnecessary disability-screening criteria also require examination. Do not declare an existing rule unchangeable merely by calling it a standard. Propose an authorized change and check whether it improves access. A planning meeting held with the family members the person chooses, at a time they can attend, with a qualified interpreter, still has to produce a plan that meets program requirements.

Adapting also has limits that matter in a public agency. Staff should not make private exceptions to rules because they understand a community well. Changes to policy go through the responsible policy and legal review. Work with the Tribal liaison to identify consultation duties and the appropriate government-to-government process. Under Minnesota Statutes 10.65, formal consultation concerns matters with Tribal implications; ordinary partner engagement does not satisfy that duty. Accommodation for disability goes through the ADA coordinator or the accommodation process. Concerns about discrimination go to EOAD. Acceptance helps you notice when those channels are needed; it does not replace them.

Leaders and supervisors can make adaptation easier. Build questions about cultural patterns into the Equity Analysis Toolkit discussions your unit already holds. Give staff permission to propose alternative methods that meet the same standard, with a clear route for approval. Close the loop with community partners by telling them what changed as a result of their input and what did not, and why. And treat adaptation as a skill that grows with practice, not a trait someone has or lacks. No one on the team should be asked to disclose their own cultural background or identity to justify a change; use authorized feedback and outcome information, explain their limits and check individual preferences. Culture is one possible consideration alongside disability access, language, resources and personal circumstances.
lessons.keyPoint: Use understanding to propose and test appropriate changes. Check both the requirement and the method with responsible staff, preserve the person’s participation, and follow applicable consultation, accessibility and policy processes.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD team is revising how people learn they may be eligible for a new self-directed service option. Samira, the team lead, has heard from a Karen community organization and a Deaf community advisory group that the planned written notice and phone line will not reach many people. Her team understands why. Now they must decide what to do before the rollout date. Ben suggests adding plain-language translated notices and a video in American Sign Language, made with the advisory group, and asking partner organizations to host information sessions. Chloe worries that doing this for some groups is unequal treatment.
lessons.question: How should Samira respond to Chloe's concern?
choices: Agree with Chloe and keep one written notice for everyone so treatment is identical.
Approve Ben's plan immediately and skip review, since the team clearly understands the communities involved.

Explain that more usable communication can support access, then route the plan through equity analysis and communications review. Ask responsible staff to confirm eligibility, accessibility and language-access requirements and any needed modifications.
feedback: An identical written notice may leave the stated access barriers unresolved. Examine what people can use and the agency’s duties; do not label Chloe’s orientation from this response.
The plan is promising, but skipping review risks errors in translation, accessibility or legal requirements, and removes accountability for the decision.

This is the strongest response. It addresses the reported barriers through the responsible review process without assuming that every existing requirement is beyond review. Test communication with intended users and explain any unresolved limits.
lessons.reflection: Think of a decision where a person or partner identified a barrier. What requirement applied, what method was customary, and who could determine whether a change or modification was appropriate?
lessons.action: Using Samira’s fictional case, identify a communication barrier and a possible change. State what the responsible staff must verify, who should help test it, and how the team could assess whether access improves.

check.question: What most clearly distinguishes Adaptation from Acceptance on the Intercultural Development Continuum?
check.correct: Adaptation includes the ability to shift perspective and adjust behavior in culturally appropriate ways, not only to recognize and appreciate differences.
wrong: Adaptation means giving up one's own cultural identity.
Adaptation means applying exactly the same approach to every group.
check.feedback: Adaptation adds the capacity to act across cultural difference in ways that are authentic and appropriate. It does not require losing one's own identity, and it moves away from, not toward, a single identical approach.

cards.back: On the Intercultural Development Continuum, an intercultural mindset in which people recognize and appreciate patterns of cultural difference and commonality in their own and other cultures.
Accepting that a cultural difference is real and makes sense in context does not mean approving of it. Judgment remains, but it is based on context rather than one's own unexamined standard.
People in Acceptance may understand a difference well yet not know how to adjust their own behavior or process in response.
Distinguish what the applicable rules actually require from the usual way of doing the work. Confirm both with responsible staff, including whether accessibility duties require a modification.
The next orientation on the continuum: the ability to shift perspective and adjust behavior in culturally appropriate and authentic ways.

aid.heading: Link learning to a decision
items: Name what the team has learned about the people this decision affects.
Identify the exact step in the process where that learning could change something.
Use the current approved agency equity analysis or scan; distinguish it from the statewide quick guide.
Tell partners what changed because of their input, and what did not and why.

aid.heading: Decide across perspectives
items: Understand each perspective in its own context before judging.
Check the requirement and method with responsible staff, including whether a modification is required.
Make and explain a decision instead of waiting for full agreement.
Anchor decisions in the person's own choices and applicable law and rules.

aid.heading: Use formal channels
items: Policy changes go through policy and legal review.
Work through the Tribal liaison on consultation duties; ordinary partner engagement does not replace formal consultation.
Disability accommodation goes through the ADA coordinator or accommodation process.
Discrimination concerns go to EOAD; never make private exceptions to rules.
